text.p: Burundi's isolated military regime began a "national debate" on Tuesday, declaring it was a first step to peace, but political leaders of the Hutu majority as well as Tutsi hardliners boycotted it.
Major Pierre Buyoya, installed by the mainly Tutsi army in a coup last year, said the debate was not a start of negotiations with Hutu rebels and their exiled leadership.
"The national debate is the first step towards the beginning of the peace process," he said in an opening speech at the thinly attended forum in the capital Bujumbura.
"We are convinced the national debate will allow us to launch a process towards a durable peace," he said, calling on absentees to change their minds and take part in the debate.
The main political party at the forum was Uprona which represents many in Burundi's 15 percent Tutsi minority and is close to Buyoya.
Regional countries clamped economic and diplomatic sanctions on Burundi last July 31, six days after the army took power.
The embargo is still in force despite regular breaches which allow some vital commodities to enter the landlocked country.

Burundi's ethnic civil war, which has claimed about 150,000 lives since 1993, has raged on since the coup. Hutu rebels led by Leonard Nyangoma's Forces for the Defence of Democracy (FDD) are waging a hit-and-run war in the countryside against the army with civilians as the main casualties.
Four rebels and three villagers were killed during a rebel attack at Gihanga, in the northwest Bubanza province, Burundi radio reported on Monday.
Last weekend the government shortened the night curfew in the capital by two hours, reflecting relative security in Bujumbura compared with the interior.
Nyangoma's exiled supporters reject the national debate as a futile exercise. They want direct negotiations with the army and their goal is majority rule by Hutus.
The mainstream Hutu party, Frodebu, also boycotted the debate saying it was a one-sided affair organised by one of the belligerent parties.

Frodebu, which won the 1993 elections by a large margin, is in disarray. Ten of its leaders still in Burundi, including parliamentary speaker Leonce Ngendakumana, are barred from leaving the country because of judicial inquiries into their alleged role in the "genocide" against Tutsis in 1993.
A party leader, ex-president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya, remains inside the U.S. ambassador's residence in Bujumbura where he took refuge two days before Buyoya's coup.
The U.S. ambassador and other senior diplomats attended the national debate's opening ceremony.

African and international diplomatic efforts to help peace in Burundi have stalled. New impetus is expected after the appointment last week of Algerian diplomat Mohamed Sahnoun as the special envoy to the troubled Great Lakes region for both the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity.
The hardline Tutsi party, Parena, also boycotted the debate on the grounds it was a pro-Buyoya talking-shop.
A South African mediator between Burundi's warring factions, Jan Van Eck, attended Tuesday's ceremony and backed the debate.

"Without dialogue it is impossible to arrive at a solution. I wish all parties would take part in this," Van Eck, a white parliamentarian representing the African National Congress (ANC), told reporters.
